sbh2.2:1.3: Asanga's sixfold taxonomy is unique to the Yogācāra and represents a substantial expansion of the four-great-elements/cemetery treatment found in VSM Ch 6 and the Vimuttimagga. The six are not six different objects — they are six different *ways of seeing* any given object as foul.
sbh2.2:3.2: Standard 32-parts contemplation, found at MN 10, DN 22, the Khuddakapāṭha, and VSM Ch 8 §44. Asanga's list matches the Pali list almost exactly. The same list appears in the *aśubhā*, *dhātu-prabheda*, and *ānāpānasmṛti* sections — one observation, three different practices, depending on framing.
sbh2.2:4.2: The canonical *aśubha-nimitta* sequence (also at MN 10 / DN 22): *vinīlaka* (discolored), *vipūyaka* (festering), *vibhadrātmaka* (bursting/bloated), *vyādhmātaka* (swollen), *vikhāditaka* (gnawed). The *vibhadrātmaka* form is unusual; the cognate *vibhadraka* may be a variant of *vipadumaka* ('worm-eaten') or could represent textual corruption.
sbh2.2:5.2: A surprising move: foulness here is not about bodies or corpses but about *painful feeling itself*. The unsatisfactoriness of *duḥkha-vedanā* is treated as a kind of foulness. The framing targets the lust-for-pleasure by exposing that the apparatus generating pleasure is the same apparatus generating pain.
sbh2.2:7.2: Relative foulness — recognizing that 'fair' is always relative. Even a blissful jhāna, even the highest formless attainment, even the very peak of existence (*bhavāgra* — the highest of the formless attainments) is foul *relative to nirvāṇa*. The contemplation for practitioners attached to meditation states.
sbh2.2:9.2: *Prabhaṅgura* — 'perishable, breaking-up.' The five aggregates of clinging are *anitya* (impermanent), *adhruva* (unsteady), *anāśvāsika* (unreliable / not-conducive-to-confidence), and have *vipariṇāma-dharmatā* (the nature of change). This is *aniccānupassanā* (contemplation of impermanence) framed as foulness.
sbh2.2:10.2: *Kāma-cchanda* / *kāma-rāga* paired throughout: *chanda* is desire (motivational attraction), *rāga* is lust (fully-developed attachment). The Sanskrit pairs them systematically.
sbh2.2:10.4: The taxonomy is hierarchical: gross to subtle. *Kāma-rāga* (sense-pleasures of the desire-realm) → *rūpa-rāga* (form-realm meditation-state lust) → *satkāya-rāga* (attachment to existence itself). The first three are the desire-realm; *rūpa-rāga* is form-realm-bound; *satkāya-rāga* operates across all realms.
sbh2.2:12.1: The therapeutic mapping of cemetery aspects to specific lusts: *varṇa-rāga* (color-lust) is dispelled by the discolored/festering/bursting/swollen contemplations. The body's color spoils.
sbh2.2:12.3: *Saṁsthāna-rāga* (form-lust, i.e., shape) is dispelled by the bloody-skeletal contemplation. The body's form reduces.
sbh2.2:12.5: *Sparśa-rāga* (contact-lust, lust for the feel) is dispelled by the bone or skeleton contemplation. The body's tactile reality reduces.
sbh2.2:12.7: *Upacāra-rāga* (approach-lust, lust for the body as a single near object) is dispelled by the dispersed contemplation. The body's unity dissolves.
sbh2.2:13.1: Asanga's cemetery aspects are read as expansions of the Buddha's four *śiva-pathikā* (charnel-ground) sections from the canonical *kāyagatā-sati* discourses (MN 10, DN 22). The practitioner is not doing something different from the Buddha's instruction — a more articulated version of the same.
sbh2.2:14.7: Asanga clarifies the scope: although the whole sixfold taxonomy is given here, *only inherent foulness* (*pratyaśubhatā*) is properly the *rāga-carita* practitioner's primary practice. The other five foulnesses are also applicable to other temperaments — *duḥkhāśubhatā* for the *duḥkha-anupassanā* practitioner, *prabhaṅgurāśubhatā* for impermanence-work, etc.
